paragraphs.text: BY THE SAME GREGORY, BISHOP OF NYSSA: ON HIS OWN ORDINATION. Our turn too has come to serve at the spiritual feast, though we are better suited to sharing what others provide than to providing for others ourselves. In fact I for my part thought it only right to be entirely excused from such contributions, because of my poverty in speaking, under a kind of law of the banquet. For I hear that people of more refined habits, when they take turns preparing the feasts for their common table, have a rule that if anyone on the list of diners is poorer than the rest, he dines with them excused from the common contribution. So I too wished to be a guest at the table of the rich. But since this good and wealthy host does not spare even us, and orders us to serve, I will say to him: "Friend, lend me your loaves." By loaves I mean the support of your prayers. For how can I welcome your ears, after they have feasted on these spiritual honeycombs, with a meagre and beggarly speech? And perhaps it would be well to do as in athletic contests, where the stadium belongs only to the strong and the rest become spectators of the competitors. So too in this spiritual stadium, only those who are vigorous in the power of the saints should strip for the contest against the competitors. But if anyone is like me, with grey hair, his strength grown sluggish with age, and his speech trembling and limping, let him be allowed to take his delight in the sweat of the contestants. Let us not, then, draw out our preface for you, brothers, lingering in our admiration of those who spoke before us. You are already full; you have already been made rich; and your fullness comes from sweet things, for the earlier speech nursed you on these. So perhaps I would be heaping useless fullness on fullness, adding to golden words and loading your memory with what are, as it were, leaden coins. And yet a poorer material mixed with a finer one often helps to bring out its beauty, and the proof is close at hand. Do you see this ceiling above our heads, how beautiful it is

to look at, how elegantly the gold blooms on its carvings? Its whole surface is golden, but underneath it is marked out with polygonal circles painted in blue. What, then, did the craftsman intend by the blue? I think it was so that the gold, seen against the contrasting colour, might shine out all the more. If, then, blue mixed with gold makes its gleam more beautiful, perhaps it is not out of place for our ink too to be set down beside the brilliance of the words already spoken. We are still chattering at you in preludes. But I hear that the great Moses, when he was setting up the tabernacle for the Israelites, together with that Bezalel who by the divine Spirit had the wisdom of architecture without being taught, offered the honour of giving to rich and poor alike: from the rich they chose gold and purple and precious stones, and from the poor they did not refuse wood and skins and goats' hair. But perhaps recalling this story is not out of place, for I want to share with everyone the thought that came running into my heart. By the divine Spirit Bezalel became wise when he had been unskilled; so the story says. Let the Pneumatomachian, then, listen. Whoever has called the Holy Spirit divine, whose coming stamps the grace of wisdom on the soul like a footprint, does he insult the dignity of the Spirit with the title "divine"? Does he suggest that we think something small and lowly about him? Which of the things in creation is signified by this name? Does he suppose that the Spirit's godhead was acquired? Does he imagine some doubleness and composition in what is simple and uncompounded? Surely it is not possible to go along with such suspicions. Rather, he certainly confesses that the Spirit, being divine by nature, both is such and is called such. You see how the truth unveils itself to you of its own accord. For the preaching of Christians knows nothing of many divine natures, since then we would be bound to invent many gods as well. It is impossible to conceive of many gods unless a difference of nature announces the plurality of the gods. If, then, all believe that there is one divine nature, and the Holy Spirit is divine by nature, why do you sever in word what is joined in nature? But who will give me the power of that speech whose outcome was the salvation of its hearers? Peter delivered a single address to the people of Jerusalem, and so many thousands of people were caught in the fisherman's net when he cast his word. Yet so many teachers, and such teachers, wear themselves out among us: what addition has there been to those being saved? "What fails, fails," says one of the prophets, "what dies, dies." The one who has strayed does not return; the bond of love has been loosed; peace has been snatched from our treasu-

-ries. O the evil of it! For I am moved to groan over this calamity. Love was our possession. This was once our ancestral inheritance, which the Lord stored up for us through the disciples when he said, "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another." Those who succeeded one another, each receiving this inheritance from his father, kept it safe down to our fathers; but this prodigal generation has not guarded it. How has the wealth of our upbringing slipped through our hands and gone? We are beggared of love, and others revel in our goods. "I was envious of the lawless," says the Psalmist. But I, altering the saying a little, will read it: "I was envious of the lawless; I was envious when I saw the peace of sinners." They stand together with one another, while we are cut off from one another. They lock shields with each other, while we break up our own wall of shields. The robber of souls has stolen our possession, carried it off and flung it to the enemies of the truth. Let no one think he did this to benefit them, for the inventor of evils cannot become a benefactor. He did it to make them worse through their agreement in evil. "But what have I to do with judging those outside?" says the one who said it. Yet how shall I bear the estrangement of our brothers without tears? How has this younger brother gone off and abandoned his father's estate? He is a different one from the son shown in the Gospel; but even if he hides the youth of his soul under the grey hair of his body, how has he gone away into a far country, running away from the faith? How has he too gone off, having halved his father's estate by dragging the lofty doctrines down to low and swinish thoughts, and squandered his wealth on heretical harlots? For heresy is a harlot, bewitching men with the pleasures they love. If only he would one day come to himself, like that son! If only he would long once more for his father's food! If only he would run back to the rich table where the daily bread is plentiful, the bread that feeds the Lord's hired servants! And all who work God's vineyard in hope of the promise are God's hired servants. What a running there would be toward him, not of one father but of so many fathers, coming to meet him, embracing him, greeting him with kisses! The first robe would be brought out, the robe of the faith, which the three hundred and eighteen souls wove as they laboured well for the Church. Then a ring for his hand, with the seal of the faith engraved on it; the dancing, the calf, the music, and everything else listed in the Gospel, except the brother's jealousy. But why do we vainly invent dreams for ourselves? The hearts of our brothers have been hardened and they resist us. They hold up our common fathers as their own, yet do not accept the inheritance that comes from them. They lay claim to our common noble descent,

yet are estranged from their kinship with us. They take their stand alongside our enemies and are hostile toward us. They have become a kind of borderland between us and our foes, and are both and neither: they do not confess the right doctrine, and yet they refuse to be called heretics. What a strange thing! They are at war equally with the truth and with falsehood, like a tree without roots, easily bending this way and that before opposing gusts. I have heard John the evangelist, in his secret revelation, speaking to such people in a riddle: that one must be thoroughly fervent in spirit and cold toward sin. "Would that you were cold or hot," he says. What is neither of these, but touches both, is nauseating and fit only for vomiting up. What, then, is the reason that of old, in the time of the disciples, a great multitude was brought into the Church through the Lord, while now people pass by the long and splendid discourses of the teachers?

Someone will perhaps say that in those days the miracles that accompanied their works assisted the apostles, and their word was made credible by the gifts of grace. I too say that the force of deeds carries great weight in persuading. But now, what are we to [?] of what is happening? Do you not see similar miracles of faith? For I count as my own the achievements of our fellow servants, since we walk by the same Spirit in the power of healing. Men who have come from beyond our borders bear witness to the truth of what I say: fellow citizens of our father Abraham, who set out from Mesopotamia. They too went out from their land and from their kindred, and from the whole world. They look toward heaven; in a way they have emigrated from human life and stand above the passions of nature. They touch this life only as far as they must, and for the greater part they journey on high together with the bodiless powers. They are aged in appearance, venerable to look upon, gleaming with grey hair, their mouths sealed with silence. They do not know how to wrangle over words; they have never learned to dispute. They have such authority over the spirits that they work miracles by their will alone, and the demons retreat, not before the arts of syllogism but before the authority of faith. The demons are not driven into the perplexity of a contradiction; they are driven out into the outer darkness. This is how the Christian knows how to reason; these are the achievements of our faith. Why, then, do we not persuade, if the grace of healing abounds, and if the teaching of the word is plentiful? All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as he wills. Why is there no addition to those being saved? And let no one suspect that I think the present grace small. I see the vine luxuriant, flourishing with branches and abounding in fruit. I see the field rippling with its multitude of ears of grain: the crop is deep, the sheaf full, the seed abundant. But what am I to do? My nature cannot be satisfied in such matters, and I am gripped by the passion of those who love wealth.

No limit of possessions brings desire to a halt. Whatever is constantly being added stirs up the appetite for more and becomes fuel for the desire of more still. What I see gladdens me. I rejoice in those who are present and grieve for those who are absent. A shared feeling made up of opposites holds my soul, pleasure blended with grief. When I look up at you, I rest my longing on you; when I reckon up what is lacking, I cannot groan enough over the misfortune. For people have stopped delighting in the Lord and rejoicing in the peace of the Church. Instead they spin technical arguments about substances and measure magnitudes, measuring the Son against the Father and granting the Father more than the measure. Who will tell them this? What has no quantity is not measured; what has no form is not assessed; what has no body is not weighed; what has no limit is not compared; and what is not compared admits no reckoning of greater and less. For it is by setting things beside one another that we recognize the greater; but where the end cannot be grasped, the greater cannot be conceived. I heard the refrain that all of us sang together in our hymn: "Great is the Lord, and great is his strength, and of his understanding there is no number." What, then, does this mean? Count what has been said, and you will understand the mystery. "Great is the Lord": he did not say how great. For it was impossible to say how much; instead, by the indefiniteness of the expression he leads the mind toward the infinite. Likewise he says, "Great is his strength": when you hear "strength," understand the Power, for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. "But of his understanding there is no number": Isaiah interprets this "understanding" clearly when he speaks of "the Spirit of wisdom and understanding." I heard in the Beatitudes that those who thirst for the Lord are called blessed. Perhaps, then, this thought is not out of season; so accept my words, even if they seem detached from present matters. Suppose someone is travelling at midday, with the sun's hotter rays scorching his head and parching with their flame all the moisture in his body; and suppose the ground before his feet is rough, hard going and parched. Then suppose such a man comes upon a spring whose stream is lovely and clear, pleasantly cool and overflowing in abundance. Will he sit down by the water and philosophize about its nature, examining where it comes from, and how, and by what means, and all the other things that idle talkers usually say: that some moisture drawn down into the depths of the earth seeps through, is compressed and becomes water; or that veins spread through the hollows below pour out water whenever they are opened? Or will he bid all such things farewell, bend over the stream, put his lips to it, relieve his thirst, refresh his tongue,

and still his longing, and give thanks to the one who gave him the gift? Imitate the thirsty man, then. Say, as indeed it has been said, "Blessed are those who thirst." And once you have learned what kind of goods, and how many, the Holy Spirit pours forth, do what the Prophet says: "Open your mouth and draw in the Spirit." Open your mouth wide and fill it, since the gifts are yours to take. Do you want to learn how many goods pour forth from the spring of the Spirit? Incorruption of soul, everlasting life, the kingdom of heaven, unceasing gladness, joy without end. But when I look at what is present, I count the loss of what is lacking as small. My house is filled with good things; the treasuries are full of the gold of Arabia. And perhaps before long envoys will come from Egypt too, and stretch out their hands to God first, and the kingdoms of the earth will sing with us the hymn of victory to the one who calls everyone into his kingdom. To him be glory and might for ever. Amen. [?] On the installation at Constantinople.
